description: We’re two friends who go way back to middle school, now teaming up to bring fresh ideas to agriculture! As something at the heart of our lives, we believe agriculture has huge potential to evolve through data and the latest technologies. Our team name, BEET Sugar, is inspired by our project’s focus on Hokkaido, where one of us currently lives. We’re excited to explore new possibilities and make a positive change in the future of agriculture!
summary:
In a world of increasingly extreme and unpredictable climate conditions, it is becoming more difficult for farmers to decide which crops to grow and how to plan their crop rotations each year.
Our team proposes Rotation Compass, a mobile-first web application that helps farmers make informed crop rotation decisions using NASA satellite imagery, historical harvest records, and climate data.
For any location on Earth, Rotation Compass transforms NASA POWER data into a climate record dating back to 1991, showing how current seasonal conditions differ from the 1991–2020 climate normal. In our demo field in Tokachi, Hokkaido, the app overlays NASA satellite imagery onto actual field parcels and compares three crop rotation options, highlighting supporting evidence, uncertainties, and factors that need to be checked locally. It also allows neighboring farmers to share their planting plans and learn from one another.
By turning NASA data into practical insights, Rotation Compass helps farmers anticipate climate conditions and prepare for the coming growing season. Ultimately, the farmer always makes the final decision.
details:
Rotation Compass

We propose a mobile-first web application "Rotation Compass" which enables farmers to gain useful information on deciding crop rotation.

What Farmers Can Do with Rotation Compass

1. Explore Maps and Fields

Farmers can select their own fields or search for any location on Earth. By switching between map layers, they can explore soil moisture (SMAP), precipitation (GPM IMERG), vegetation health (MODIS NDVI; HLS at 30 m when zoomed in), snow cover, and soil types. Official NASA GIBS color maps and field markers help them understand local conditions.

2. Understand Historical Climate and Harvests

For each season, farmers can explore 30+ years of climate, soil conditions, and historical harvest data. The app compares the earlier 10 years (2005–2014), the recent 10 years (2015–2024), and a selected year, with charts showing changes over time. By selecting any year on the 1991–2027 timeline, farmers can see what made that season unusual and which crops performed well under similar conditions, based on government’s yield data. (For the demonstration of Tokachi, data of Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries (MAFF) of Japan is used as government’s yield data.)

3. Explore This Year's Conditions and Harvest Potential

Using this year's climate and soil conditions, farmers can explore potential harvest outcomes and understand how current conditions may affect different crops. Rather than relying on a single prediction, the app provides insights to help farmers assess their options.

4. Get Three Crop Rotation Recommendations with AI Advisor (Scripted Demo)

Farmers can select up to two priorities: income, workload, soil health, water use, or marketability. Based on these priorities and the available climate and harvest data, Rotation Compass presents three crop rotation options: continuing the current rotation, switching crops, or planting green manure before wheat.

Each option is compared side by side, with information organized into four categories:

  • Evidence: What the available data tells us
  • Benefits: Potential advantages of the option
  • Information gaps: What we still don't know
  • Needs local review: What farmers should check before making a decision

The "If that year came again" feature also replays three historically unusual seasons (1993: cold, 2016: wet, and 2023: hot) to compare how each rotation option performed under similar conditions.

5. Look Ahead with Climate-Based Insights

The app provides practical insights for planning upcoming agricultural activities. For example, it identifies the latest workable sowing date for hairy vetch (green manure) after wheat, based on a threshold from the Hokkaido Research Organization and NASA POWER daily temperature data. In our demonstration, this timing worked in 9 out of 10 historical years.

Note: These insights are based on historical climate patterns and thresholds, not actual weather forecasts.

6. Check Government Outlooks and Support

Farmers can also explore government outlooks, including crops that may face declining production and related subsidy or support programs. This information can help farmers consider not only climate conditions but also broader agricultural trends and financial support when planning their next crop. The government information view is currently a concept demonstration.

7. Share Planting Plans with Neighbors

Farmers can register the crops they plan to grow next year and view the planned crop distribution within a 10 km radius. This helps them identify potential overproduction of the same crops in their area and anticipate shared resource demands, such as busy grain dryers. By sharing information with neighboring farms, farmers can make more informed decisions and potentially avoid excessive concentration of the same crops in one area.

Note: Neighboring farmers' planting data in our demo is dummy data.

How We Keep Our Recommendations Scientifically Honest

Rotation Compass aims to support, not replace, farmers' knowledge and judgment. Every recommendation is accompanied by its supporting evidence, potential benefits, information gaps, and points requiring local verification. We distinguish historical climate-based insights from actual weather forecasts and make uncertainties visible rather than presenting AI-generated recommendations as guaranteed outcomes.

Ultimately, Rotation Compass gives farmers more information and perspectives to consider, while leaving the final decision in their hands.
